name: Gjallarhorn
appearance: Large divine horn; depicted on Isle of Man stone cross and Gosforth Cross; figure holding horn and sword
significance: Heimdallr's horn; when sounded will herald Ragnarök; sound heard in all corners of the world; also used to drink from Mímir's well of wisdom

name: Oliphant
appearance: Ornate ivory war horn; drinking vessel
significance: Roland's legendary horn from Song of Roland; sounded at Battle of Roncevaux; iconic medieval chivalric artifact

name: Shofar
appearance: Ram or kudu horn; curved; no mouthpiece mechanics
significance: Ritual horn for Jewish new year and Yom Kippur; also signaled battle commencement and troop movements; sounded at fall of Jericho (biblical)
notes: Living religious tradition flag — Jewish; player-facing naming caution

name: Chazozra (Hebrew Trumpet)
appearance: Straight silver trumpet; used alongside shofar in Jerusalem Temple
significance: Distinguished from shofar; straight metal trumpet; Temple ritual and military signaling

name: Pututu
appearance: Shell or cow horn; conch trumpet
significance: Andean signaling instrument; messengers (chaski) used it to announce arrivals; also ceremonial

name: Dungchen
appearance: Long ritual horn (several meters); played at temples
significance: Tibetan Buddhist ceremonial horn; deep resonant tone used in ritual practice
notes: Living religious tradition flag — Tibetan Buddhism

name: Lehel's Horn
appearance: Preserved horn attributed to chieftain Lehel; kept in Jászberény, Hungary
significance: Horn of Magyar chieftain Lehel; historical artifact; national Hungarian legend

name: Carnyx
appearance: Bronze elongated S-shaped trumpet approximately 1.8m tall; bell shaped as open-mouthed boar or animal head; held vertically in battle
significance: Celtic war instrument; incites troops and intimidates opponents; documented by Polybius; ceremonial use also evidenced (Deskford carnyx)

name: Dord (Celtic trumpet)
appearance: Celtic trumpet; revived in modern times
significance: Another type of Celtic trumpet alongside the carnyx

name: Cornu (Roman)
appearance: Approximately 3 meters long; G-shaped bronze instrument; spiral design; copper-tin bell; crossbar for shoulder support
significance: Roman military signal instrument; regulated movement of standards; played by cornicen; also used in gladiatorial games and religious ceremonies honoring Dionysus and Cybele

name: Buccina (Roman)
appearance: J-shaped instrument; derived from animal horn form
significance: Roman military signal instrument; sounded the classicum (reserved for commander-level signals)

name: Roman Tuba
appearance: Straight bronze trumpet
significance: Roman military trumpet; signaled charges, retreats, and troop movements; religious ritual use also

name: Lituus (Roman/Etruscan)
appearance: Hook-belled wind instrument
significance: Cavalry signal instrument; also used in funeral ceremonies and augury; adapted from Etruscans

name: Salpinx
approx_date: referenced in Homer (9th-8th century BCE); Classical period frequent use
appearance: Straight narrow bronze tube with bone mouthpiece and bell; 0.8-1.57m length
significance: Greek military signal instrument; tactical commands to troops across battlefield; summons for battle; used in Olympic games to signal start of chariot races

name: Lur (Scandinavian)
appearance: Long natural horn without finger holes; 1.5-2 metres; straight or curved; wooden versions covered in birch or willow
significance: Bronze Age: ceremonial (found deposited in pairs in bogs); Medieval: war instrument to marshal troops and frighten enemy; also used by farmers for cattle-calling

name: Brudevælte Lurs
appearance: Pair of matching bronze lurs; deposited in bog; matching curvatures for playing together
significance: Best-known named archaeological lur pair; found in bog northeast of Lynge, Zealand, Denmark

name: Golden Horns of Gallehus
appearance: Double-layered gold sheets; longer horn: 75.8 cm long, 10.4 cm opening, 3.2 kg; cast figures soldered onto rings; Proto-Norse Elder Futhark runic inscription
significance: 5th-century sacral gold horns; runic inscription names maker (Hlewagastiz); Germanic ritual/sacred objects; ceremonial drinking or blowing horns

name: Shanka (Hindu Conch Horn)
appearance: Conch shell trumpet; Vishnu's divine conch
significance: Holy symbol of Vishnu; can declare war; used in Hindu religious life for centuries; sacred instrument of the highest order
notes: Living religious tradition flag — Hinduism; substrate only for sacred-context conch

name: Montes Bocineros Horns
appearance: Five mountain-top horns
significance: Five horns atop Basque mountains used to summon people to General Council meetings; civic signaling use

name: Lituus (Etruscan predecessor)
appearance: Similarly curved trumpet to carnyx; Etruscan form
significance: Likely inspired carnyx design; Etruscan ancestor of Roman lituus
